Every claim made for an AI system is a statistical claim. An accuracy rate, the savings from a pilot and the share of customers who would use a new agent are all estimates from a sample, and every estimate carries error. In my analysis of a national health survey, one model was 88.7% accurate and still found almost none of the people it was built to find,[@nsduh-analysis] which is the kind of number that statistics exists to catch.

## What the plus in AI+ stands for

The site's name reads as AI, plus the data science, math, statistics and Python behind it. The Visual Handbook's second chapter sets out how those parts fit: statistics makes sense of data, machine learning learns patterns to predict, and data science combines the two with code and domain knowledge to deliver something useful.[@vb-ch2] Statistics asks why a pattern exists, and machine learning asks what comes next.[@vb-ch2]

Statistics runs through every stage of an AI system, from collecting the right data to measuring whether the system works once it is live.[@vb-ch2] A large language model is the clearest case, because it writes by estimating the probability of each possible next word and choosing a likely one.[@vb-ch2] When a vendor or a team reports a number about such a system, the number is a statistic, and it can be tested like one.

## Questions that test an AI number

Three questions catch most of the ways a number misleads. The survey analysis shows each failure on real data, drawn from 134,897 adults in three years of the National Survey on Drug Use and Health.[@nsduh-analysis]

| Question | What goes wrong without it | What it looked like in the survey analysis |
|---|---|---|
| Compared with what? | An accuracy rate can reflect how rare the outcome is more than how good the model is | 88.7% of adults reported no depressive episode, so a model that answered "no" to almost everyone scored 88.7% accuracy |
| Measured on whom? | A sample that over-represents some groups misstates the population | Unweighted, 11.29% reported a past-year depressive episode, and weighted to the population the figure was 8.44% |
| How sure? | Ignoring how the sample was drawn makes estimates look more precise than they are | Standard errors that respect the survey design were 1.74 to 1.96 times larger, so naive intervals were about half as wide as they should be |

: Three questions to ask of any AI number, with the failure each one caught in a real analysis

The same discipline applies to the model's own scorecard. A model's accuracy is a proportion, so it carries a margin of error exactly as a poll does.[@vb-ch74] That margin shrinks with the square root of the test set, which means halving it takes four times as many labeled examples.[@vb-ch74] A leaderboard number reported without its margin tells you less than it appears to.

None of the three questions needs advanced mathematics. Each needs a habit of asking before a number goes into a decision, and each has a standard answer that a careful analyst can produce.

## What to do next

1. **CIO.** Ask for the baseline with every accuracy figure, meaning the score of a model that always gives the most common answer.
2. **CTO.** Require a margin of error, and the sample behind it, on any model metric that decides whether a system ships.
3. **Analyst.** When a sample over-represents some groups, report the figure weighted to the population and say which figure answers the question being asked.
